writtenBy: Traditional French round; music sometimes attributed to Jean-Philippe Rameau (unproven). English words traditional
aboutKids: Brother John is still fast asleep in bed, so everyone sings to wake him up because the morning bells are ringing.
story: A French round about a sleepy friar who should be ringing the bells for early prayers. Its earliest known source is a French manuscript of about 1775-1785, where it is titled Frere Blaise; it was first printed in 1811. A scholar has found evidence linking the music to Rameau, but authorship is unproven.
funFact: Composer Gustav Mahler turned the tune into a slow, minor-key march in the third movement of his First Symphony.
myth: A claim that the song is about the 17th-century surgeon Frere Jacques Beaulieu has no supporting evidence. Who wrote the round, and why, is unknown.
catalogNote: Catalog says printed c.1780. The c.1780 source is a manuscript (dated c.1775-1785 by the Bibliotheque nationale, titled Frere Blaise); the first known printing is 1811 (James Fuld). Public-domain status is unaffected.

writtenBy: Traditional British singing game
aboutKids: Children hold hands in a circle and skip around, then put a hand, a foot or their head in the middle and shake it.
story: A traditional circle game in which players put in and shake each body part in turn. The Opies found the dance known by 1745; Robert Chambers printed a text in The Popular Rhymes of Scotland, and Alice Gomme recorded versions in 1894. It spread to America, Ireland and New Zealand, and may be an ancestor of the Hokey Pokey.
funFact: Looby Loo was the name of a singing rag doll in the BBC puppet show Andy Pandy, first broadcast in 1950.
catalogNote: Earlier than Gomme (1894): the Ballad Index cites a text in Chambers' Popular Rhymes of Scotland (1870 edition), and the Opies date the dance to at least 1745. Gomme lists the game under the title Lubin. Strengthens the public-domain basis.

writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: traditional, first printed by J. W. Elliott (1870)
aboutKids: Little Bo-Peep cannot find her sheep anywhere. She learns that if she waits patiently, they will wander home all by themselves.
story: An English nursery rhyme. A manuscript of about 1805 holds the first verse, and the fuller version was printed in Gammer Gurton's Garland in 1810. Bo-peep, an old name for peekaboo, is centuries older than the rhyme. The familiar tune was first printed by James William Elliott in 1870.
funFact: Bo-peep, the old English name for peekaboo, was already played in Shakespeare's time; he mentions it in King Lear.
myth: Hidden meanings have been proposed (the English Civil War, the Jacobites, Mary Queen of Scots, smuggling), but none is proven, and the rhyme is not recorded before about 1805.
catalogNote: Consistent. Slightly earlier records exist: a c.1805 manuscript of the first verse (Wikipedia) and an 1806 printing cited by the Opies (Ballad Index), both before Gammer Gurton's Garland (1810).

writtenBy: Traditional English counting song
aboutKids: A cheerful old man counts all the way from one to ten, tapping out a rhythm on something new for every number.
story: A traditional counting song that began as a children's singing game. Folk-song scholar Anne Gilchrist remembered a version learned from her Welsh nurse in the 1870s. Baring-Gould and Sharp printed a version in English Folk-Songs for Schools (1906), and Malcolm Arnold's arrangement for a 1958 film turned it into a pop hit.
funFact: The Barney theme song I Love You is sung to this same old tune.
catalogNote: The 1906 English Folk-Songs for Schools printing is supported only by Wikipedia; the library records checked list no contents. Gilchrist learned it from a Welsh nursemaid and published her note in 1937; Cecil Sharp also collected it in Norfolk in 1911. The NOTES-content.md file cited in publicDomainBasis does not exist in the repo.

writtenBy: Traditional African American lullaby (Southern United States)
aboutKids: A grown-up gently rocks a little one to sleep, promising lovely horses of every color to play with in the morning.
story: A traditional lullaby from the American South, widely believed to be of African American origin. Its earliest known printing is in Maud Lindsay's 1903 kindergarten story A White Dove, which calls it an old lullaby. Dorothy Scarborough found it widely sung across the South in 1925, and John and Alan Lomax published it in 1934.
funFact: Its first known printing was tucked inside a 1903 story for kindergarten children by Maud Lindsay, an Alabama teacher.
myth: It is often described as a lullaby sung by enslaved women to the white children in their care, as Scarborough (1925) and others wrote. This is plausible, but no 19th-century record survives to confirm it.
catalogNote: Resolves the catalog's unverified print date: earliest print found is 1903 (Maud McKnight Lindsay, A White Dove), per Wikipedia; the Ballad Index's earliest source is 1918 (Cecil Sharp). Both pre-1931, consistent with the public-domain basis. Nineteenth-century circulation is inferred, not documented.

writtenBy: Words: traditional singing game. Tune: Austrian folk song O du lieber Augustin
aboutKids: One child in the circle does a silly move, everyone else copies it, and then someone new gets a turn to lead.
story: A singing game in which a leader acts out a motion and the circle copies it. The tune is the Viennese song O du lieber Augustin, first published around 1800. Despite the Scottish words lassie and laddie, the game was first collected in the United States in the 1890s; a print appears in Jessie Bancroft's Games for the Playground (1909).
funFact: Despite its Scottish-sounding words, the game was first written down in America and was not found in Britain until the mid-1900s.
myth: It is often called a Scottish folk song because of the words lassie and laddie, but it was collected in the US first. The story that the tune is about the Viennese bagpiper Marx Augustin (1679) is a legend.
catalogNote: Catalog says the words were printed in the US by the 1890s and calls it Scottish/American. Sources say it was first collected in the US in the 1890s, with the earliest cited print in 1909 (Bancroft); a Scottish origin is doubtful. Tune date c.1800 confirmed.

writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: J. W. Elliott (1870)
aboutKids: A little mouse scampers up a tall clock. When the clock strikes one, he gets a surprise and scurries back down.
story: First printed in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book (London, 1744), the first collection of English nursery rhymes, spelled Hickere Dickere Dock. The nonsense opening may come from counting-out games; some link it to old Westmorland shepherds' words for eight, nine and ten. The usual tune was published by J. W. Elliott in 1870.
funFact: Exeter Cathedral's clock door has had a cat-sized hole since 1598, so the cathedral cat could slip in and chase mice.
myth: The rhyme is often said to be about Exeter Cathedral's astronomical clock and its cat door. The cat door is real, but no evidence links it to the rhyme.

writtenBy: Traditional English dance tune; earliest sheet music Jullien & Co. (1853), arranged by George Thompson
aboutKids: A playful weasel and a cheeky monkey dash round and round, and everyone waits for the big pop at the end!
story: It began as a fashionable social dance that swept England in late 1852; dancers sang the title line while ducking under each other's arms. The earliest known sheet music, from Jullien & Co., dates from 1853, and American editions followed that year. Words were added around 1854-55, and the verses kept changing for decades.
funFact: Before it was a nursery song, it was a grown-up dance craze in 1852, taught in dance schools and played at fancy balls.
myth: The popular claim that weasel is Cockney rhyming slang for coat (weasel and stoat), so the song is about pawning a coat, is unproven. That slang is documented only from the 1930s, and in the 1850s nobody seemed to know what the line meant.
catalogNote: Catalog says published 1852 and calls it a music-hall tune. It was a dance craze from 1852, but the earliest known printed music is 1853 (Jullien & Co.); the music-hall link comes from later verses about London venues. Public-domain status is unaffected.

writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: traditional, in J. W. Elliott (1870)
aboutKids: A king and queen sit down to a special pie, and when it is opened, a whole flock of blackbirds starts to sing!
story: The first verse appeared in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book (London, 1744), though with a different filling than blackbirds. A version with birds was printed around 1780, the four-verse rhyme by 1784, and happier extra endings were added in the 1800s. Possible earlier allusions in Shakespeare and in Beaumont and Fletcher are uncertain.
funFact: Birds in a pie were a real party trick: a 1549 Italian cookbook explains how to bake a pie so live birds fly out.
myth: The claim that the pirate Blackbeard used the rhyme as a secret recruiting code is false; Snopes invented it in 1999 as a deliberate spoof. Other hidden meanings (Henry VIII, the calendar) are unproven.

writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme
aboutKids: A duke leads ten thousand marching soldiers all the way up a big hill, and then all the way back down again.
story: Its oldest relative is Old Tarlton's Song, printed in 1642 and credited to the Elizabethan clown Richard Tarlton, about a King of France marching his army up a hill. A Duke of York version was noted in Warwickshire in 1892, and the modern words were printed in Arthur Rackham's Mother Goose (1913). It is a favorite action song.
funFact: The oldest known version, from 1642, was about a King of France, not a duke, and his army was even bigger.
myth: The duke is often said to be Prince Frederick, Duke of York, in the 1793-94 Flanders campaign, or Richard, Duke of York, in 1460. No evidence links the rhyme to either.
catalogNote: Catalog calls Rackham's 1913 Mother Goose 'an early form'; it is the first printing of the modern form. The earliest related text is Old Tarlton's Song (1642), and a Duke of York version was noted in 1892.

writtenBy: Words: Traditional American. Tune: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
aboutKids: Someone hurries off to tell Aunt Rhody some sad news about her old gray goose, who leaves her little goslings behind.
story: The melody began as a wordless dance in Jean-Jacques Rousseau's 1752 opera Le devin du village. It spread through Britain and America, became the hymn tune Greenville around 1825, and was later sung with American folk words about Aunt Rhody's goose. Folklorists, including Cecil Sharp, collected those words in the early 1900s.
funFact: The tune was written by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the famous French philosopher, as a dance in his 1752 opera.
myth: The tune is often called Rousseau's Dream, as if it came to him in a dream. The name comes from J. B. Cramer's piano variations and a mix-up with a different Rousseau piece.
catalogNote: Catalog dates the American song to the 1840s; no source found confirms that. The earliest documented Aunt Rhody texts are c.1913 (Journal of American Folklore) and 1918 (Sharp). The 1752 Rousseau melody is confirmed.

writtenBy: Traditional English street cry
aboutKids: Long ago in London, sellers walked the streets calling out about warm, sweet buns with a cross on top, sold for just a penny.
story: It began as a London street cry: sellers called out to sell spiced buns on Good Friday, when shops were shut, a cry recorded in Poor Robin's Almanack in 1733. The words appeared as a round in the London Chronicle in 1767 and in the Christmas Box in 1798. Today it is often a child's first tune.
funFact: The artist Thomas Rowlandson drew a London bun seller calling out this very cry in a 1799 print, now in the London Museum.
myth: A popular story says a monk in St Albans baked the first cross buns in 1361. There is no evidence for it, and the name hot cross buns is first recorded in 1733.
catalogNote: Catalog gives the Christmas Box (1798) as the print source; an earlier printing exists in the London Chronicle, June 1767. Public-domain status is unaffected.

writtenBy: Tune: traditional German folk melody (Hanschen klein). English words: anonymous
year: 1784 or earlier (tune); English words printed by 1914
aboutKids: A family glides along in a little boat, rowing gently over calm, sparkly water on a bright, sunny day.
story: The melody is an old German folk tune: the earliest evidence is a dance tune written down in 1784, and Franz Wiedemann's words Hanschen klein (1860) made it a German children's favorite. American school songbooks set English boating words, Lightly Row, to it; one version appears in Hollis Dann's First Year Music (1914).
funFact: Lightly Row is one of the very first pieces in the Suzuki violin method, coming right after Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.
catalogNote: Catalog dates the melody to the 19th century; the earliest evidence is a manuscript dance tune dated 30 June 1784 (German Wikipedia, citing Erk and Bohme). The German words are by Franz Wiedemann (1860). The earliest English Lightly Row print confirmed is 1914; the 19th-century songbook claim was not verified.

writtenBy: Antonio Vivaldi (music); English words by Little Duet
aboutKids: Spring is here! Birds sing, a little storm rumbles past, and then the birds start singing again, played by happy violins.
story: Spring is the first of Vivaldi's four violin concertos known as The Four Seasons, composed around 1718-1720 and published in Amsterdam in 1725 in his collection Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione. Each concerto comes with a sonnet, possibly by Vivaldi himself, describing the scenes the music paints, an early example of storytelling in music.
funFact: In Spring, the violins imitate singing birds, and the music follows a poem line by line, even pausing for a thunderstorm.

writtenBy: Gioachino Rossini
aboutKids: Fast, bouncy music that sounds like horses galloping. Trumpets call, and the whole orchestra races to an exciting finish!
story: Rossini wrote the overture for Guillaume Tell, his last opera, which premiered in Paris in 1829 and tells the Swiss legend of William Tell. The overture has four parts played without a break; the famous final gallop is known as the March of the Swiss Soldiers. Rossini lived 39 more years without writing another opera.
funFact: The gallop became the theme music of The Lone Ranger on radio and TV, so many people picture a cowboy riding to the rescue.
myth: The finale is widely heard as a cavalry charge or horse race, but the opera has no horses or cavalry in it; the section is the March of the Swiss Soldiers.

writtenBy: Traditional French folk song; English words by Little Duet
aboutKids: Under the bright moon, a friend knocks on a neighbor's door to ask for a pen and a little light.
story: An 18th-century French folk song whose writer is unknown. The earliest printing found is from 1820, and fuller versions appeared in French song collections in 1858 and 1870. Its gentle, simple tune has made it a favorite first piece for beginners, and composers from Clementi to Debussy and Satie have borrowed it.
funFact: In 1860, French inventor Edouard-Leon Scott de Martinville recorded himself singing it: the oldest known recording of a recognizable human voice.
myth: When the 1860 recording was first played back in 2008, many reports said a young girl was singing. It had been played at double speed; at the right speed, it is almost certainly Scott himself.
catalogNote: Catalog says printed c.1780s; the earliest printing found is 1820 (Les Voitures versees). The song is generally dated to the 18th century, which still supports the public-domain basis.

writtenBy: Stephen Foster
aboutKids: Horses race round and round a long track all day and all night, while the crowd cheers and everyone sings along.
story: Stephen Foster wrote it in 1850 for the minstrel stage, and F. D. Benteen of Baltimore published it that February as Gwine to Run All Night, or De Camptown Races. Christy's Minstrels made it a nationwide hit. Its original lyrics were written in a stereotyped dialect; modern versions use standard words.
funFact: Camptown may be a real village in Pennsylvania that Foster knew from his school days nearby.
catalogNote: Consistent. Editorial flag: the song was written for blackface minstrel shows and its original lyrics used a racist dialect. The catalog's standard-spelling words avoid this, but the history may warrant care in parent-facing copy.

writtenBy: Words: Emily Huntington Miller (adapted from her poem). Music: James R. Murray
aboutKids: A child whispers a secret Christmas wish to Santa Claus, hoping for special presents to be left while everyone is asleep.
story: The words grew from Lilly's Secret, a poem by Emily Huntington Miller in the children's magazine The Little Corporal in December 1865. The tune is credited to American composer James R. Murray and was published in School Chimes (1874). The song in its familiar form was printed in 1881 and has been a Christmas favorite ever since.
funFact: The song began as a poem called Lilly's Secret in a children's magazine, published in December 1865.
myth: The words are sometimes credited to Benjamin Hanby, who wrote the similar Up on the Housetop, or to John Piersol McCaskey; the evidence points to Emily Huntington Miller.
catalogNote: Catalog calls the tune traditional; it is credited to James R. Murray, first published in School Chimes (1874). Published in 1874, it is public domain either way. The c.1865 date for the words matches Miller's poem (December 1865).

writtenBy: Traditional African American spiritual
origin: St. Helena Island, South Carolina Sea Islands
aboutKids: Friends row a boat across the water together, pulling their oars in time and singing to help them reach the shore.
story: Charles Pickard Ware wrote it down during the Civil War on St. Helena Island, South Carolina, where freedpeople sang it while rowing; his cousin William Francis Allen heard it on Station Creek in 1863. It was published in Slave Songs of the United States (1867). Tony Saletan's 1954 adaptation spread it through the folk revival.
funFact: In 1961 a folk group called The Highwaymen took the song to number one in both the United States and Britain.
myth: Pete Seeger is often thought to have written or arranged the modern version; he learned it from Tony Saletan in 1954 and credited him.
catalogNote: Catalog says Georgia Sea Islands; it was noted on St. Helena Island in the South Carolina Sea Islands. The 1867 publication in Slave Songs of the United States is confirmed.

writtenBy: Edvard Grieg (music); English words by Little Duet
aboutKids: The sun slowly rises and the music grows brighter and brighter, like a big, sleepy yawn and stretch at the start of the day.
story: Grieg wrote it in 1875 as part of his music for Henrik Ibsen's play Peer Gynt, which premiered in Christiania (now Oslo) on 24 February 1876. It is the prelude to Act IV, and Grieg later made it the opening movement of his Peer Gynt Suite No. 1, published in 1888.
funFact: It sounds like a Norwegian sunrise, but in the play it is a dawn in the desert of Morocco.
myth: It is often thought to picture a sunrise over Norway's fjords; in Ibsen's play it accompanies a desert dawn in Morocco, where Peer Gynt is stranded.
